title: Seven Days That Divide the World
author: lennox

entries.title: God Speaks the Universe Into Being (Genesis 1:1)
entries.content_summary: For Lennox, Genesis 1:1 is the load-bearing sentence of the entire biblical worldview. Its claim is metaphysical before it is anything else: the universe is not eternal, not self-generating and not self-explanatory, but was called into existence by a personal God who is himself uncreated. Before there was space, time or matter, God already was, and 'in the beginning God created the heavens and the earth' announces that reality itself has both a beginning and a Maker. Everything that exists is therefore contingent, dependent moment by moment on the will of the One who spoke it into being. Against every attempt to treat the cosmos as ultimate, or to say it simply is without cause or purpose, Genesis roots all that exists in the free, intentional, creative word of God.
entries.content_detail:
Lennox treats Genesis 1:1 not as primitive myth but as a majestic, deliberately simple statement of the deepest truth about reality: that the physical universe is derivative, dependent and made. The verb 'created' places God prior to and distinct from his creation, so that the heavens and the earth are neither an emanation of God nor a rival eternal principle, but the product of his will. This immediately rules out both the ancient notion of self-originating matter and the modern claim that the universe is simply a brute fact requiring no explanation.

Central to Lennox's reading is that creation happens by God speaking. The repeated 'and God said' shows that behind the cosmos stands not blind force but mind, word and intention, a rational Creator whose speech brings ordered reality into being. This is why, for Lennox, the universe is intelligible and open to scientific study: a word-spoken world reflects the rationality of the One who uttered it. Personhood, not impersonal law, is the ultimate ground of things.

Lennox also stresses what Genesis 1:1 does not do. It does not argue for God's existence but assumes it, and it does not compete with physics on physics' own terms. It answers a different and prior question: why there is something rather than nothing, and to whom it belongs. Read this way, the opening verse frames the entire narrative that follows. The God who begins the story as Creator is the God who will act in history, and the reader is invited to receive the account as true testimony about origins rather than as one creation-legend among many. The confession that God made the heavens and the earth becomes, for Lennox, the foundation of a coherent view of the world, of human dignity, and of meaning.

entries.title: 'In the Beginning' as an Initial, Undated Creation Before the Days
entries.chapter_or_episode: Genesis 1:1 and the relationship to the six days
entries.content_summary: One of Lennox's distinctive contributions is his reading of the relationship between Genesis 1:1 and the six days. He argues that the opening verse records an initial act of creation, the bringing into being of the universe, that is not itself dated and is not necessarily part of the first day. On this view the six days of divine activity begin only at verse 3, so an unspecified stretch of time may lie between the original creation of the heavens and the earth and the sequence of days that follows. The immediate consequence is that the age of the universe is simply left open by the text: whatever figure the sciences propose, Scripture has not tied the antiquity of the cosmos to the length of the six days. The narrative can still be read as fully historical without committing the reader to a recent creation.
entries.content_detail:
Lennox notes that Hebrew grammar does not require the events of Genesis 1:1 to be collapsed into day one. The first day is introduced with its own 'and God said' at verse 3, which allows one to take verse 1 as a self-standing statement: God first created the heavens and the earth, and only afterwards is the six-day sequence narrated. Verse 2 then describes the state of the already-created earth before God begins his ordered work of forming and filling.

He is careful to distinguish this from the older 'gap theory,' or ruin-reconstruction view, which imagined a cosmic catastrophe and a fall of Satan filling the interval between verses 1 and 2. Lennox does not build his case on any such speculative catastrophe. His point is more modest and textual: the initial creation is undated, so the antiquity of the universe is not something the passage settles. A believer may therefore accept the vast ages indicated by physics and geology without feeling that loyalty to Scripture is at stake.

Crucially, for Lennox this is not a concession that empties the text of history. He continues to read Genesis as authoritative and as making real claims about real events: a genuine beginning, a real ordering of the world, a real first human pair. What he resists is the assumption that faithfulness requires reading the days as fixing the age of everything. By locating the age question in the undated creation of verse 1 rather than in the six days, he aims to free the reader from a false choice between trusting the Bible and accepting well-established results about the age of the cosmos. The teaching that God is the Creator stands firm; the timetable is, he argues, left deliberately and legitimately open.

entries.title: The Days as a Real Sequence of God's Creative Acts, Not a Test of Young-Earth Chronology
entries.content_summary: Lennox surveys the main ways Christians have read the six days: as six consecutive twenty-four-hour days, as long ages, as a literary framework, and as days of divine creative action. He declines to make any one of them a test of faithfulness. The recurring 'evening and morning' marks the days as a real, ordered sequence of God's creative speech, and Lennox takes the account as genuine history rather than myth or allegory. But he argues that the text itself does not compel the young-earth conclusion that the days must be six consecutive ordinary days of a recently made world. The days may be understood as a patterned sequence of divine acts, possibly separated by longer periods. What matters is that God really spoke and really made; the precise chronology is a secondary, legitimately disputed question.
entries.content_detail:
In weighing the options, Lennox treats the twenty-four-hour view with respect but not as the only possible literal reading. He points out that the sun is not said to be set in place until day four, which complicates the assumption that days one to three must be measured by ordinary solar rotation, and he notes that the seventh day is not closed with the 'evening and morning' formula at all, features that have long led careful readers to ask what kind of days are in view.

His own preference leans toward reading the days as real days on which God spoke and acted, without insisting that they were an unbroken run of six ordinary days at the dawn of a young earth. On such a reading the days structure the account and convey a true sequence of divine creative activity, while the total span of cosmic and geological time is left to the undated creation of verse 1. He is equally clear, however, that he holds no interpretation dogmatically and regards several of these readings as compatible with a high view of Scripture.

Throughout, Lennox insists that taking Genesis as historical does not require a wooden literalism, and that reading the days flexibly is not the same as treating them as fiction. The narrative asserts real events in a real world: light, sky, land, vegetation, luminaries, creatures and humankind each brought into being by God's word, in an order that moves from formlessness to fullness. What he asks the reader to distinguish is the plain and central teaching, that God is the sole Creator of an ordered world, from the contested secondary question of exactly how long the process took. On the latter he counsels conviction held with humility, and warns against allowing a particular chronology to become the measure of orthodoxy.

entries.title: The Galileo Lesson: Distinguishing Scripture From Our Interpretation of It
entries.content_summary: To show why the age-of-the-earth debate should not divide believers, Lennox turns to the Galileo affair. Galileo's opponents cited biblical texts that speak of the earth being fixed and unmovable, 'the world also is established, that it cannot be moved' (Ps 93:1; cf. Ps 104:5; 1 Chr 16:30), and treated the moving-earth cosmology as an attack on Scripture. History showed that those texts had been read through the scientific assumptions of the day; they were poetic and phenomenological, and did not in fact teach a stationary earth. Lennox draws the lesson carefully: we must distinguish what Scripture actually teaches from a particular interpretation of it, and we must not make a secondary matter, then the earth's motion, now the age of the earth, into a test of orthodoxy or of loyalty to the Bible.
entries.content_detail:
Lennox's use of Galileo is deliberately even-handed. He is not scoring points against traditional belief; he is warning every party in the creation debate against the mistake the seventeenth-century church made. That mistake was not believing the Bible too much but confusing one interpretation of the Bible with its actual teaching. Verses such as Psalm 93:1, Psalm 104:5 and 1 Chronicles 16:30 describe the earth as firmly established and not to be moved. Read as though they were astronomy, they seemed to rule out a moving earth; read as the vivid, phenomenological language of worship, they say nothing of the kind, and the church eventually recognised this.

The application to Genesis is direct. Just as the fixed-earth reading turned out to be an interpretation rather than the necessary meaning of the text, so a particular reading of the days may be an interpretation rather than the plain teaching of Scripture. Lennox is emphatic that this cuts in every direction: it is a caution to old-earth and young-earth advocates alike against absolutising their own construal and then judging the faith of others by it.

He couples this with a distinction he returns to often: the difference between the central message of a passage and the disputed details surrounding it. On the age and mechanism of creation, Christians of undoubted seriousness have long disagreed, and Lennox argues that such disagreement should be held within fellowship, not made a boundary marker of true belief. The authority of Scripture is not in question; what is in question is the humility with which we interpret. His plea is for conviction without dogmatism, to hold one's reading honestly while refusing to bind another's conscience, or to imply that trusting the Bible depends on accepting a particular date for the world. The Galileo story stands as a sober reminder of what happens when interpretation is mistaken for revelation.

entries.title: Humanity Made in the Image of God (Genesis 1:26-27)
entries.content_summary: Genesis 1:26-27 is, for Lennox, the charter of human dignity. Alone among the creatures, humankind is made 'in the image of God,' male and female alike, and given a place of responsible dominion over the created order. Lennox reads this as a decisive answer to every reductionism that would treat human beings as nothing but animals, machines or accidental arrangements of matter. To bear God's image is to be a person capable of relationship, reason, moral responsibility and stewardship, a creature who reflects, however imperfectly, the character of the Creator. This confers a worth that does not depend on utility, ability or status, and grounds the equal dignity of every human being. The verse thus underwrites both the value of the individual and the vocation of humanity to care for the world on God's behalf.
entries.content_detail:
Lennox draws attention to the solemn deliberation that precedes the creation of humankind, 'let us make man in our image,' which sets it apart from the preceding acts of creation and signals that something distinctive is happening. The image is conferred on humanity as such: 'male and female he created them,' so that the dignity in view belongs equally to men and women, not to one sex or class.

To be made in God's image, on Lennox's reading, is not primarily about physical form but about capacities and calling that mirror the Creator: rationality, moral awareness, the ability to love and to relate, and a delegated authority to rule and steward the earth. The dominion granted in verse 26 is therefore not licence to exploit but a trust to be exercised responsibly, under God and on his behalf.

Much of the force Lennox finds here is apologetic, but he keeps it anchored to the text. If human beings are the image-bearers Genesis says they are, then the reductive account that describes them as merely complex biochemistry, or as survival machines programmed by their genes, fails to reckon with what they most deeply are. The worth of a person cannot then be measured by usefulness, intelligence, health or productivity; it rests on a status conferred by God at creation and shared by all.

Lennox also sees in this verse the foundation of a coherent ethic. Human rights, the obligation to treat others as ends rather than means, and the special gravity of taking human life all follow naturally if humans bear the divine image, and are left hanging if they do not. In a culture tempted either to inflate humanity into its own god or to deflate it into an accident, Genesis 1:26-27 holds the balance: creatures, yet crowned with a God-given dignity and responsibility that nothing in the natural order can account for on its own.

entries.title: Creation Pronounced Very Good: Goodness and Rational Order (Genesis 1:31)
entries.content_summary: Genesis closes its account of the six days by pronouncing the whole 'very good' (Gen 1:31), and Lennox makes much of this verdict. The world is not an illusion, not evil, and not a chaotic accident, but a good and ordered cosmos that its Maker delights in. The repeated refrain that each stage is 'good,' rising to 'very good' at the end, presents creation as coherent, purposeful and fundamentally positive. Lennox connects this goodness and order to the very possibility of science: a rational, intelligible universe is what one would expect from a rational Creator, and the ordered structure of Genesis 1, separating and then filling day by day, mirrors that intelligibility. The goodness of the original creation also sets the stage for everything that follows, including the problem of evil, since the world as God made it began good.
entries.content_detail:
Lennox notes the deliberate rhythm of the chapter: at successive stages God sees that what he has made is good, and at the climax, surveying the whole, he pronounces it 'very good.' This is a value judgment placed in the mouth of the Creator himself, and it shapes the biblical attitude to the material world. Matter is not a prison or an illusion to be escaped, as in various ancient and modern philosophies; it is God's good handiwork, to be received with gratitude and cared for.

Equally important for Lennox is the order the chapter displays. The six days move in a patterned way from formless emptiness toward structure and fullness: realms are separated, light from darkness, waters above from waters below, sea from land, and then populated with lights, creatures and finally humankind. This is not chaos slowly stumbling into shape but the work of a mind, producing a cosmos, an ordered whole, rather than a disordered heap.

Here Lennox links Genesis to a theme he presses elsewhere: the rational intelligibility of the universe. Science proceeds on the conviction that the world is orderly and can be understood, and Lennox argues that such intelligibility is exactly what one would expect if a rational God made the world by his word. The goodness and order of Genesis 1 thus underwrite, rather than compete with, the scientific enterprise.

Finally, the 'very good' verdict has theological weight for what comes next. Because the world began good, evil and suffering are intruders rather than original features of creation; they enter a good world and spoil it, which is why the biblical story can speak of redemption and of a restored creation. Lennox is careful to keep this tied to the text: the goodness pronounced in Genesis 1:31 is the baseline against which the later disruption of the fall, and the hope of renewal, are to be understood.

entries.title: Creation Through the Word and the Son (John 1:1, 1:3; Colossians 1:16)
entries.chapter_or_episode: Genesis read through the New Testament
entries.content_summary: Lennox insists that Genesis must be read in the light of the New Testament, which identifies the God who spoke creation into being as the eternal Word. John opens his Gospel by echoing Genesis, 'in the beginning,' and declares that the Word was with God and was God, and that 'all things were made by him' (John 1:1, 1:3). Paul says the same of Christ: 'by him were all things created,' in heaven and on earth (Col 1:16). For Lennox this means the personal Word who created is the very one who became flesh in Jesus. Creation is therefore Christ-centred: the universe was made through him and for him, and the rational order that makes the cosmos intelligible has its source in a personal Logos rather than in impersonal law or blind chance.
entries.content_detail:
Lennox reads John 1 as a deliberate theological commentary on Genesis 1. John's opening words consciously repeat 'in the beginning,' and where Genesis says 'and God said,' John names the one who speaks: the Word, who was with God and was God, and through whom all things came into being. Nothing that exists came to be apart from him. For Lennox this identifies the creative speech of Genesis with a personal agent, the Logos, and so answers the question of what, or rather who, lies behind the ordered universe.

Paul's language in Colossians 1:16 reinforces the point: all things, visible and invisible, in heaven and on earth, were created through Christ and for him, and in him they hold together. Creation is thus not only from God and through the Word but also toward a purpose centred on Christ. The universe has a goal, not merely an origin.

Lennox draws two conclusions he cares about deeply. First, the ultimate explanation of the cosmos is personal. If the Word is the agent of creation, then mind and meaning are not late by-products of matter but are woven into the foundations of reality; the world is the expression of a rational, purposeful person. This, he argues, makes far better sense of the universe's intelligibility, and of the existence of rational, meaning-seeking creatures within it, than an account that begins with the impersonal.

Second, the Creator is not remote. The Word through whom the worlds were made is the one who entered his own creation and became flesh. Lennox sees this as the deepest answer to human questions about God's care: the God who made everything is not a distant first cause but has come near in Christ. Genesis and the Gospel thus belong together. The God who begins the Bible as Creator is revealed at its centre as the incarnate Word who upholds and redeems what he has made.

entries.title: By Faith We Understand: Reasoned Trust in the Creator (Hebrews 11:3)
entries.content_summary: Hebrews 11:3, 'through faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God,' gives Lennox his account of how creation is known. He is at pains to correct the caricature that faith is belief without evidence, or belief against evidence. Biblical faith, he argues, is a reasoned trust that leads to understanding, not a leap in the dark; the verse pointedly links faith with understanding. To grasp that the universe was made by God's word, and that the visible came from what is invisible, is an insight of faith that is nonetheless rational and illuminating. Far from being the enemy of thought, faith here opens the mind to the true origin of things. Lennox thus reads Hebrews 11:3 as a charter for the harmony of faith and reason and for creation out of nothing.
entries.content_detail:
Lennox fastens on the wording of Hebrews 11:3: it is by faith that we understand. Faith and understanding are not set against each other here; faith is the means by which a genuine understanding is reached. This lets him challenge the widespread modern assumption, which he attributes especially to certain popularisers of atheism, that faith by definition means believing where there is no evidence. On the contrary, he argues, the faith the Bible commends is trust grounded in evidence and testimony, more like the well-placed confidence we extend to a trustworthy person than like credulity.

The content of this understanding is striking: the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible. Lennox reads this as an early and clear statement of creation out of nothing. The visible order does not derive from some prior visible stuff but from the invisible God and his word; the material rests on the immaterial, the physical on the personal.

He connects this to his broader case that faith and reason are allies rather than enemies. The same word of God that framed the worlds is the word that faith trusts, and the intelligibility of those worlds is part of the evidence that invites such trust. To perceive design, order and contingency in the universe and to conclude that it was made is not irrational; it is, Lennox contends, the reasonable response to what is there.

He is careful, however, not to reduce this to mere inference. Hebrews speaks of understanding that comes through faith, a knowing that engages the whole person in trust toward God, not only the intellect assembling an argument. The origin of the universe, on this account, is finally grasped not by unaided calculation but by faith that is itself reasonable, a faith that receives the testimony that God spoke, and in receiving it comes to understand where everything came from.
